questions.question: To prove a property holds for every ordinal below ε₀, a proof covers three cases: 0, successor ordinals from the predecessor, and limit ordinals from all smaller ordinals. Which induction principle is being used?
questions.explanation: Transfinite induction generalizes induction to well-ordered sets like the ordinals, splitting the step into successor and limit cases.

questions.question: A proof that every vector space has a basis argues: any chain of linearly independent sets has a union that is still linearly independent — an upper bound — so a maximal linearly independent set exists. Which lemma is invoked?
questions.explanation: Zorn's lemma: if every chain in a partially ordered set has an upper bound, the set has a maximal element — here, a basis.

questions.question: To select one representative from each member of an infinite family of nonempty sets, a proof simply asserts a choice function exists, since no uniform rule for choosing can be defined. Which axiom licenses the move?
questions.explanation: The axiom of choice states the product of a family of nonempty sets is nonempty — a choice function always exists.

questions.question: To show no list r₁, r₂, r₃, … exhausts the reals, a proof constructs a number whose n-th digit differs from the n-th digit of rₙ, so it differs from every listed number. What is this technique called?
questions.explanation: Cantor's diagonal argument builds an object differing from the n-th enumerated object in the n-th feature, escaping any enumeration.

questions.question: To prove Σₖ C(n,k) = 2ⁿ without algebra, a proof counts the subsets of an n-element set twice: once by size k, and once by deciding membership element by element. Which proof style is this?
questions.explanation: A combinatorial (double-counting) proof establishes an identity by showing both sides count the same set.

questions.question: To prove a graph with a certain Ramsey property exists, a proof computes that a uniformly random graph enjoys the property with probability greater than 0 — hence some graph has it — without constructing one. Which non-constructive method is this?
questions.explanation: The probabilistic method, pioneered by Erdős, proves existence by showing a random object has the desired property with positive probability.

questions.question: To show x⁴ + y⁴ = z² has no positive integer solutions, a proof derives from any alleged solution a strictly smaller positive solution, contradicting that the naturals cannot decrease forever. Which method did Fermat use here?
questions.explanation: Infinite descent refutes existence by showing any solution spawns a smaller one, violating the well-foundedness of ℕ.

questions.question: Every finite subgraph of an infinite graph is 4-colorable. Encoding 'vertex v gets color c' as propositional atoms and invoking the compactness theorem, a proof concludes the whole graph is 4-colorable. What is this style of reasoning called?
questions.explanation: A compactness argument extends a property from all finite substructures to the infinite whole via the compactness theorem: the coloring axioms are finitely satisfiable, hence satisfiable.

questions.question: In a proof assistant, the goal (a+b)² = a²+2ab+b² is closed by rewriting the left side step by step — expand, commute, collect — until it is syntactically the right side. Which proof method is this?
questions.explanation: Equational reasoning proves identities by a chain of justified equalities or rewrites transforming one side into the other.

questions.question: A lattice proof of x∧(x∨y) = x is mirrored line by line — meets become joins and the order flips — to obtain x∨(x∧y) = x for free. Which proof method exploits this symmetric structure?
questions.explanation: Duality in lattice/Boolean contexts swaps the two operations and reverses order, turning any valid proof into a proof of the dual statement.

questions.question: Naive set theory allows forming S = {x : x ∉ x}. Asking whether S ∈ S yields a contradiction either way, destroying unrestricted comprehension. Which paradox is this?
questions.explanation: Russell's paradox: the set of all sets that do not contain themselves both must and cannot contain itself, refuting naive comprehension.

questions.question: To produce a model of ZFC where the continuum hypothesis fails, Cohen enlarges a countable transitive model by adjoining generic sets and controls which statements the extension satisfies via a forcing relation. Name the technique.
questions.explanation: Forcing, introduced by Paul Cohen (1963), extends models of set theory with generic objects and yields independence results such as the failure of CH.

questions.question: To let arithmetic speak about its own syntax, a proof assigns each symbol a number and encodes a formula's symbol sequence via prime powers — e.g., 2ᵃ·3ᵇ·5ᶜ — so syntax becomes arithmetic. What is this encoding called?
questions.explanation: Gödel numbering (arithmetization) encodes formulas and proofs as numbers so a theory can reason about provability internally.

questions.question: To prove a rewrite system terminates, a proof runs induction over a well-founded order: since the relation admits no infinite descending chains, each case may assume the property for all smaller elements. Which principle generalizes induction this way?
questions.explanation: Well-founded (Noetherian) induction: if a relation has no infinite descending chains, one may prove P(x) assuming P(y) for all y below x.

questions.question: A verifier annotates a program with triples {P} C {Q} meaning 'if P holds before C executes, then Q holds afterward'. Which formal system verifies programs with such assertions?
questions.explanation: Hoare logic reasons about {precondition} program {postcondition} triples via rules for assignment, sequencing, conditionals, and loops.

questions.question: To prove 'if n² is even, then n is even' by contraposition, what assumption must the proof start with?
alternatives: assume the conclusion fails: n is odd
questions.explanation: The contrapositive of p→q is ¬q→¬p: assume n is odd and derive that n² is odd.

questions.question: In the induction step for 1+2+…+n = n(n+1)/2, what exactly is the inductive hypothesis that the proof may assume?
alternatives: assume the formula holds for n = k
the statement is true for some k
questions.explanation: The hypothesis assumes P(k); the step must then derive P(k+1), i.e. sum to k+1 equals (k+1)(k+2)/2.

questions.question: The classic proof writes √2 = a/b in lowest terms and derives that a is even and then b is even. What is the actual contradiction that finishes the argument?
questions.answer: a and b share a common factor of 2
alternatives: both a and b are even, contradicting lowest terms
the fraction a/b was not in lowest terms
questions.explanation: Lowest terms means gcd(a,b)=1, but both being even forces a shared factor of 2 — a contradiction.

questions.question: A proof by cases splits the argument on whether p holds or ¬p holds. Which classical law legitimizes this exhaustive split?
questions.explanation: p∨¬p is a tautology, so the two cases cover every possibility — nothing is missed.

questions.question: A minimal-counterexample proof assumes a counterexample exists and takes the smallest one. Which property of ℕ licenses picking a smallest element?
alternatives: every nonempty subset of ℕ has a least element
questions.explanation: Well-ordering guarantees every non-empty subset of ℕ has a least element, so a smallest counterexample exists to be examined.
